question: Switzerland's old-age insurance system is built on a three-pillar structure. Which combination correctly names the three pillars?

options.A: State provision (OASI) and occupational provision (pension funds) only
options.B: State provision, occupational provision, private provision, and a fourth universal pillar for low-income households
options.C: State provision (OASI), occupational provision (pension funds) and private provision
options.D: State provision (OASI), mandatory employer pensions and mandatory private savings for every employee

source_quote:
The Swiss old-age insurance system is based on three pillars: state provision (OASI),
occupational provision (pension funds) and private provision.
notes: Swiss-specific: the AHV / BVG / Pillar-3a triad has no direct EU equivalent. Germany has state plus occupational pensions only and no third pillar.

question: A person who has just moved to Switzerland and is not yet enrolled with a Swiss health insurer must arrange compulsory basic health insurance cover within what period?

options.A: Within one month of arriving
options.B: Within two months of arriving
options.C: Within six months of arriving
options.D: Within three months of arriving

source_quote: If you have just moved to Switzerland, you have three months in which to arrange
notes: The same three-month deadline applies to new-borns, and the person or baby is already insured during that period. This is a Swiss KVG rule, not an EU social-security coordination rule (do not import the EU three-month rule or the EU residence-condition logic).

question: In Switzerland, a policyholder who wants to switch compulsory basic health insurer for the following calendar year must have the cancellation letter received by their current insurer by which date?

options.A: 15 October
options.B: 30 November
options.C: 15 December
options.D: 31 December

source_quote: Your letter must reach your current health insurer by 30 November.
notes: The 'Stichtag 30. November' is uniquely Swiss. Note the separate mid-year cancellation right that only holders of the CHF 300 standard deductible enjoy (tested separately in this category).

question: In Switzerland, a healthy adult who chooses the highest available compulsory basic health insurance deductible should set aside how much per year in order to be able to cover their own maximum share of healthcare costs?
source_quote:
You should still put CHF 3,200 aside in case you do fall ill
(CHF 2,500 deductible and CHF 700 retention fee).
notes: CHF 3,200 = highest adult deductible CHF 2,500 + CHF 700 maximum annual retention fee. A German/EU reader is likely to think only of a deductible.

question: Under Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, an adult holds the standard annual deductible of CHF 300. What is the maximum that this adult can end up paying out of pocket for healthcare in one calendar year?

options.A: CHF 700

source_quote: In other words, for an insured person with an annual deductible of CHF 300, the maximum cost share is CHF 1000 per calendar year.
notes: Key anti-trap item: CHF 1,000 is the MAXIMUM ANNUAL COST SHARE (CHF 300 deductible + CHF 700 maximum retention fee), not a deductible band. Distractor A is the retention-fee cap alone.

question: In Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, which set of optional annual deductible levels may adults choose from?
source_quote: For adults, the available deductibles are 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 francs, and for children 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 and 600 francs.
notes: Levels are chosen voluntarily; there is no age / income ('affluence') / rural-residence rule assigning a band. Distractor B is the children's list.

question: Under Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, a policyholder wants to raise their deductible to CHF 1,500. Which statement correctly describes the insurer's legal obligation here?

options.A: The insurer must offer the CHF 1,500 level, because it is one of the standard adult deductible levels
options.B: The insurer is not required to offer the full range of deductible levels and may offer only some of them
options.C: The insurer must offer it, but only if the policyholder is under 25 years old
options.D: The insurer must offer it, but may charge an additional administration fee

source_quote: The health insurer does not have to offer the full range of deductibles.
notes: Insurers MAY also differentiate for young adults aged 19-25. Corrects the widespread misconception that Swiss deductible levels are assigned by rule.

question: A Swiss compulsory health insurance policyholder opts for a deductible higher than the standard CHF 300, which reduces his premium. The premium reduction is capped by law at what share of the additional risk the policyholder assumes?

options.A: 70 per cent
options.B: 50 per cent
options.C: 90 per cent
options.D: 100 per cent

source_quote: A maximum of 70 percent reduction on the additional risk assumed by the policyholder may be granted.
notes: Statutory ceiling on the additional-risk discount. It is a separate rule from the statutory minimum-premium floor and must not be conflated with it.

question: Swiss law requires every compulsory health insurer to charge a floor below which the premium may not fall. What is that statutory minimum premium set at, relative to the premium the insurer would ordinarily charge?

options.A: 30 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region
options.B: 70 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region
options.C: 80 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region
options.D: 50 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region

source_quote: The health insurer is required to charge a minimum premium equivalent to 50 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the age group and premium region of the person concerned.
notes: The floor cannot be undercut even by policies excluding accident cover or restricting the choice of service provider. Prevents insurers competing on restricted-benefit products.

question: In Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, a policyholder wants to move from the standard CHF 300 deductible to a higher optional deductible. When can that change take effect?

options.A: At any time during the year, on 30 days' notice
options.B: Only at the beginning of a calendar year
options.C: From 1 April, when insurers recalculate their premiums
options.D: Immediately, provided the policyholder has had no treatment in the current year

source_quote: A change in the level of the deductible can only take effect at the beginning of a calendar year.
notes: The deductible level is locked to the calendar year, unlike, for example, switching insurers. Do not confuse with the separate end-of-June cancellation right for CHF 300 deductible holders (S019).

question: A holder of the CHF 300 deductible under a 'regular' insurance model in Switzerland wants to leave their current compulsory basic health insurer outside the ordinary year-end round. When can the cancellation take effect, and on what notice?

options.A: End of March, on one month's notice
options.B: End of July, on three months' notice
options.C: End of June, on three months' notice
options.D: End of September, on six months' notice

source_quote: cancel your basic insurance with effect from the end of June. A three-month notice period
notes: This mid-year cancellation window is tied specifically to holding the CHF 300 standard deductible; it is an exception to the ordinary 30 November deadline. No foreign analogue exists.

question: In Switzerland, a daily contribution towards the cost of a hospital stay is payable by the patient. Which groups are exempt from that contribution?

options.A: Children, young adults in education and training, and pregnant women
options.B: Children and pensioners
options.C: Everyone under the age of 25
options.D: Only women receiving maternity-related services

source_quote:
Children, young adults in education and training
and pregnant women do not pay any contribution to hospital costs.
notes: The contribution itself is CHF 15 per day. Distractor C over-extends the 'young adults in education and training' exemption (which is not simply 'under 25').

question: In Switzerland, an employee is unable to work because of an accident. From when, and at what level, is an accident daily allowance payable?

options.A: From the first day after the accident, at 100 per cent of salary
options.B: From the third day after the accident, at 80 per cent of salary
options.C: From the eighth day after the accident, at 90 per cent of salary
options.D: From the fifteenth day after the accident, at 80 per cent of salary

source_quote:
as of the third day following your
accident you are entitled to a daily allowance corresponding to 80% of your salary.
notes: Swiss UVG accident insurance. If the insurer's allowance is below 80%, the employer must make up the difference. German sickness-benefit schedules (e.g. the 6-week Lohnfortzahlung) are not the relevant frame.

question: In Switzerland, a person works 5 hours a week for an employer and is covered by the compulsory accident insurance scheme. What does that accident cover include?

options.A: Occupational accidents and occupational illnesses only; accidents during leisure time are not covered
options.B: Occupational accidents and occupational illnesses as well as non-occupational accidents occurring in leisure time
options.C: No accident cover at all, because anyone working under eight hours a week must insure privately
options.D: All accidents, including those during private leisure activities

source_quote: If you work for less than eight hours a week for your employer, your accident insurance
notes: The 8-hours-per-week threshold is the UVG dividing line: at or above it, leisure-time accidents are also covered. Accidents on the way to and from work count as occupational. This is a Swiss statutory test, not an EU social-security coordination rule.

question: Under Swiss compulsory accident insurance, what minimum degree of disability must be assessed before an injured person can qualify for an accident disability pension?

options.A: At least 5 per cent
options.B: At least 20 per cent
options.C: At least 10 per cent
options.D: At least 70 per cent

source_quote:
You must be classified as at least
10% disabled to qualify.
notes: The accident disability pension may be awarded in addition to a pension under the state IV/AI disability scheme. Distractor D (70%) is the separate BVG exclusion threshold for compulsory occupational pension cover.

question: According to the Federal Social Insurance Office, what was the maximum annual tax-deductible Pillar 3a contribution in 2025 for a self-employed person who has compulsory occupational pension (BVG) cover?
source_quote: - CHF 7,258 for employees/self-employed persons with occupational pension cover;
notes: TIME-SENSITIVE: figure explicitly labelled 2025, so the year is stated in the stem. For a person WITHOUT occupational cover the 2025 limit is 20% of earnings up to CHF 36,288. Distractors B and C are BVG entry-threshold figures from other years, not Pillar 3a limits.

question: Under the AVS/AHV 21 reform in force in Switzerland since 1 January 2024, the ordinary retirement age for women is being raised in three-month steps by birth cohort. What reference age applies to a woman born in 1962?

options.A: 64 years and 6 months
options.B: 64 years and 3 months
options.C: 64 years and 9 months
options.D: 65 years

source_quote: - women born in 1962: 64 years and 6 months;
notes: TIME-SENSITIVE and cohort-locked: born 1961 = 64y3m, 1962 = 64y6m, 1963 = 64y9m, born 1964 or later = 65. The reference age is 65 for men and for women born 1964 or later; the former general women's age of 64 is superseded and must never be presented as the current rule.

question: Under the Swiss compulsory occupational pension (2nd pillar), a member's accumulated old-age assets are converted into an annual old-age pension using a conversion factor that applies identically to men and women. What is that conversion factor?
source_quote: basis of a conversion factor of 6,80% for men and women.
notes: Swiss decimal-comma notation. A single gender-neutral conversion factor is a distinctive feature of the reformed BVG and has no direct EU analogue.

question: In Switzerland, what is the maternity allowance during the 14 weeks of maternity leave following a birth?

options.A: 80 per cent of the mother's earnings, with no upper daily limit
options.B: 90 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 300 per day
options.C: 80 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per day
options.D: 100 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per week

source_quote:
Maternity allowance amounts to 80% of your
earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per day.
notes: Highly Swiss-specific 14-week / 80% / CHF 220-per-day package. Cantonal provisions, personnel regulations and collective employment contracts may provide more generous arrangements. Do not substitute EU maternity-benefit rates.

question: How does Swiss second-parent (co-parental) leave differ from maternity leave in the way it may be taken?

options.A: It must be taken as one uninterrupted block within three months of the child's birth
options.B: It is flexible: it may be taken all at once or as individual days, but must be taken within two years of the child's birth
options.C: It must be taken in full before the mother returns to work
options.D: It is flexible: it may be taken all at once or as individual days, but must be taken within six months of the child's birth

source_quote:
Unlike maternity leave, paternity/co-parental leave is flexible. You can take
it all at once, or as individual days as long as it is taken within the
notes: Co-parental leave runs for two weeks: 14 daily allowances and ten days off work, paid at 80% of earnings capped at CHF 220/day. It must be used within six months of the birth.

question: Under the conditions listed on ch.ch, how many months must a mother have been insured under the OASI/DI scheme before the birth to be entitled to maternity allowance?

options.A: Nine months prior to the birth
options.B: Three months prior to the birth
options.C: Twelve months prior to the birth
options.D: Twenty-four months prior to the birth

source_quote: You were insured under the OASI/DI scheme for the nine months prior to the birth.
notes: Traps the OASI/AHV lettering variant (the page says OASI/DI here, OASI/AHV on the paternity side) and the 3/6/12/24-month alternatives a non-expert would guess.

question: Within what period after giving birth is a mother in Switzerland not allowed to return to work?

options.A: The first four weeks after the birth
options.B: The first eight weeks after the birth
options.C: The first twelve weeks after the birth
options.D: The first six weeks after the birth

source_quote: You are not allowed to return to work in the first eight weeks after the birth.
notes: Traps confusion with the 14-week maternity leave itself and with the 16-week dismissal protection; 4/6/12 weeks are the plausible wrong figures.

question: Under which circumstance is a Swiss mother's period of claimable maternity benefits extended, and by how much at most?

options.A: If the newborn must stay in hospital for more than 21 days directly after the birth, extended by a maximum of 56 days
options.B: If the newborn must stay in hospital for more than 14 days directly after the birth, extended by a maximum of 28 days
options.C: If the newborn must stay in hospital for more than 14 days directly after the birth, extended by a maximum of 56 days
options.D: If the newborn must stay in hospital for more than 28 days directly after the birth, extended by a maximum of 84 days

source_quote: If your newborn has to stay in hospital for more than 14 days directly after the birth, the period for which you can claim maternity benefits is extended by a maximum of 56 days, provided that you return to work when your maternity leave ends.
notes: Two-figure item (trigger threshold + extension). Distractors shift either the 14-day hospital trigger or the 56-day extension while keeping the other number right, and the last one shifts both. Also traps the unpaid two-week extension as a distractor-shaped confusion.

question: A mother in Switzerland extends her maternity leave by the two weeks available beyond the standard 14-week period. What does she receive for those two additional weeks?

options.A: Maternity allowance at half the usual rate
options.B: The same maternity allowance as for the first 14 weeks
options.C: Maternity allowance at 80% of earnings, capped at CHF 220 per day
options.D: Nothing - no benefits are paid for the two additional weeks

source_quote: You have the right to extend your maternity leave by two weeks beyond the standard 14-week period. However, you will not receive benefits for those two additional weeks.
notes: Traps the 80%/CHF 220 allowance figures lifted from the standard maternity allowance rule; the extension is unpaid.

question: In Switzerland, if the mother dies within 14 weeks of the child's birth, how much further leave is the surviving spouse entitled to?

options.A: A further 14 weeks
options.B: A further two weeks
options.C: A further four weeks
options.D: A further eight weeks

source_quote: If the mother dies within 14 weeks of the child's birth, the surviving spouse is entitled to a further 14 weeks' leave.
notes: Traps the mirror-image rule on the same page: if the father or spouse of the mother dies within six months, the mother gets only two additional weeks. 'two weeks' is the confident wrong pick.

question: Which group is not subject to the mandatory Swiss LPP/BVG occupational benefits scheme?

options.A: Salaried persons with a job contract of unlimited duration
options.B: The self-employed
options.C: Salaried persons working at least 50 per cent of full time for a company
options.D: Salaried persons on contracts longer than three months

source_quote: Certain groups of people are not subject to the mandatory scheme: the self-employed, salaried persons with a job contract that does not exceed three months, family members of a person operating an agricultural establishment in which they are employed, persons who are disabled to at least 70 % according to the provisions of the AI.
notes: The other three exempt groups (short contracts, agricultural family members, 70 % disabled) are real exemptions, so a distractor naming any of them would also be defensible; instead the distractors name categories that ARE covered, which is what a non-expert would wrongly believe.

question: Under the Swiss LPP/BVG, from what point are additional retirement savings made for an employee?

options.A: From the employee's 17th birthday
options.B: From 1 January after the employee reaches the age of 20
options.C: From 1 January after the employee reaches the age of 24
options.D: From the employee's 18th birthday

source_quote: The obligation to take out insurance sets in with gainful employment, after reaching 17 at the earliest. Until the employee reaches the age of 24, contributions only cover the risks of death and disability. From 1 January after the employee reaches the age of 24, additional savings are made for the retirement pension.
notes: Traps the two other ages on the same passage (17 = entry into the scheme, 18 = entry into savings elsewhere framed), and the off-by-one of 'at 24' vs 'from the 1 January after 24'.

question: How does the Swiss state contribute to the financing of second-pillar pension funds?

options.A: By paying a fixed share of each fund's annual expenditure
options.B: By guaranteeing the conversion factor used when the accumulated capital is turned into a pension
options.C: By paying a direct per-person annual subsidy into the fund of the person's employer
options.D: Only indirectly, by granting tax exemption on the contributions and on second-pillar assets

source_quote: The state contributes only indirectly to the financing of pension funds, by granting tax exemption on the contributions and 2nd pillar assets.
notes: Traps the assumption that the state co-funds the second pillar like it does the first; tax exemption is the only state support the page describes.

question: Under the collective financing principle of the LPP/BVG, what must an employer's contribution be?

options.A: At least equal to the sum of contributions paid by all the employees
options.B: At least half of the sum of contributions paid by all the employees
options.C: Equal to that individual employee's contribution and to no more
options.D: Any amount agreed with the fund, provided it is disclosed in the fund's accounts

source_quote: The LPP/BVG is based on the principle of collective financing: the contribution of the employer must be at least equal to the sum of contributions paid by all the employees.
notes: Traps the common belief that the employer pays exactly the employee's own share, and the 50/50-style split that belongs to OASI.

question: Under the LPP/BVG, early retirement is possible from the age of 63, but an occupational benefits institution may set a lower qualifying age. How low may that age go?
source_quote: Early retirement is possible from the age of 63. Occupational benefits institutions may stipulate a lower age at which benefits can be received (but no earlier than 58).
notes: Traps the same page's maximum deferral age of 70 and the reference age of 65; 55/57/60 are plausible floors a non-expert would propose.

question: Who is covered by the mandatory Swiss old-age and survivors' insurance (OASI) scheme?

options.A: Only Swiss citizens who reside in Switzerland
options.B: Only persons in paid employment in Switzerland
options.C: Anyone who lives or works in Switzerland, regardless of nationality, including people not in paid work
options.D: Only Swiss citizens and cross-border commuters who are in paid employment

source_quote: As a general rule, anyone who lives or works in Switzerland, regardless of their nationality, is covered by the mandatory old-age and survivors' insurance scheme. You are also covered if you are not in paid work, e.g. stay-at-home spouses and students.
notes: Traps the citizenship test and the paid-employment test - the two most common non-Swiss assumptions about a national insurance scheme.

question: Under the OASI, from when must a person resident in Switzerland pay contributions, and how does that differ for someone already in paid work?

options.A: From 1 January after turning 18 in all cases; for those already working, from 1 January of the year in which they turn 16
options.B: From 1 January after turning 25 in all cases; for those already working, from 1 January of the year in which they turn 20
options.C: From the age of 20, but only for those in paid employment; non-employed persons begin at 25
options.D: From 1 January after turning 20; for those already working, from 1 January of the year in which they turn 18

source_quote: If you live or work in Switzerland, you must pay OASI contributions from 1 January after you turn 20 until you reach the reference (retirement) age. If you are already working, this obligation begins on 1 January of the year in which you turn 18.
notes: Two-age item with an inverted rule: the working person starts EARLIER (18) than the general rule (20). Distractors transplant 16/20/25 and impose a paid-employment condition the page rejects.

question: According to the Federal Social Insurance Office, what is the range of the full OASI old-age pension for a person with a complete contribution record?

options.A: CHF 1,260 to CHF 2,520
options.B: CHF 1,140 to CHF 2,280
options.C: CHF 1,260 to CHF 3,780
options.D: CHF 880 to CHF 2,520

source_quote:
- minimum old-age pension: CHF 1,260
- maximum old-age pension: CHF 2,520
notes: Traps moving one endpoint only - a CHF 880 minimum is the plausible older figure and CHF 3,780 is 1.5x the maximum.

question: How are OASI contributions shared between an employee and the employee's employer in Switzerland?

options.A: The employee pays two thirds and the employer pays one third
options.B: The employee pays half and the employer pays the other half
options.C: The employer pays the whole contribution
options.D: The employee pays one quarter and the employer pays three quarters

source_quote: - As an employee, you pay half of the contributions. Your employer pays the other half.
notes: Traps an employer-heavy split borrowed from BVG reasoning (where the employer must at least match the employees' total), which is the natural wrong assumption here.

question: Up to what annual income does the mandatory Swiss occupational pension scheme (BVG) provide cover?
source_quote: You are subject to mandatory occupational pension contributions if you annually earn more than CHF 22,680 (as of 2025) from one employer and are older than 17 (insurance cover against the risks of invalidity and death from the age of 17; old-age insurance cover from the age 25). The mandatory insurance scheme covers annual incomes up to CHF 90,720.
notes: Tests the upper coordination ceiling, not the CHF 22,680 entry threshold; CHF 45,360 is 2x the threshold and a plausible confusion.

question: What is the range of deductibles available to adults in Swiss compulsory basic health insurance?

options.A: CHF 100 to CHF 2,000
options.B: CHF 300 to CHF 4,000
options.C: CHF 0 to CHF 2,500
options.D: CHF 300 to CHF 2,500

source_quote: The lowest deductible for adults is CHF 300, the highest CHF 2,500.
notes: Traps shifting either endpoint; the CHF 0 lower bound is the child rule on the adjacent sentence.

question: Which deductibles apply to children in Swiss compulsory basic health insurance?

options.A: Between CHF 0 and CHF 600
options.B: Between CHF 100 and CHF 500
options.C: Between CHF 300 and CHF 1,000
options.D: Between CHF 0 and CHF 300

source_quote: The lowest deductible for adults is CHF 300, the highest CHF 2,500. Deductibles of between CHF 0 and CHF 600 apply for children.
notes: Traps transferring the adult band onto children and halving the child ceiling (S046 states children pay no deductible at all under the standard option, so CHF 0-300 is a confident wrong pick).

question: Once the annual deductible has been used up in Swiss compulsory health insurance, what share of healthcare costs does the insured person still pay?

options.A: Twenty per cent, capped at CHF 1,400 per year
options.B: Ten per cent, capped at CHF 700 per year
options.C: Ten per cent, with no annual cap
options.D: Five per cent, capped at CHF 350 per year

source_quote: When the deductible has been used up you will still pay ten percent of your healthcare costs. However, this retention fee is limited to CHF 700 per year (CHF 350 for children).
notes: Two-figure item (coinsurance rate + annual cap). CHF 350 is the child cap, a confident wrong pick for an adult; 'no cap' is the other common misconception.

question: How much does a hospitalised patient in Switzerland contribute per day towards the cost of a hospital stay?

options.A: CHF 5 per day
options.B: CHF 25 per day
options.C: CHF 15 per day
options.D: CHF 50 per day

source_quote: You must pay the contribution to hospital costs if you are hospitalised. It is CHF 15 per day.
notes: Traps treating the hospital daily contribution as a German-style flat daily fee; the page gives it as a fixed CHF, not a percentage.

question: Premiums for compulsory basic health insurance in Switzerland are lower for which group?

options.A: People over the age of 65
options.B: Employees who work at least eight hours per week
options.C: Insured persons who choose the CHF 2,500 deductible
options.D: Children and young adults under the age of 25

source_quote: Premiums are lower for children and young adults under the age of 25.
notes: Traps the pensionable-age intuition that premiums fall after 65, which is where most countries' premium relief goes.

question: In Switzerland, which group must take out personal accident insurance itself?

options.A: The self-employed
options.B: Salaried employees who work from home
options.C: Registered unemployed people who receive unemployment benefits
options.D: Trainees

source_quote: It you are self-employed you must take out personal accident insurance.
notes: The quote reproduces the page's grammatical slip ('It you') verbatim. Distractors are the three groups the same page says are automatically covered by an employer, Suva or the trainee scheme.

question: A registered unemployed person in Switzerland who receives unemployment benefits is automatically insured against accident by which body, and how is the premium paid?

options.A: The person's health insurer, with the premium added to the monthly health insurance premium
options.B: The Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund (Suva), with the premium deducted from the unemployment benefits
options.C: The Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund (Suva), with the premium paid by the person's employer
options.D: The cantonal authority, with no premium charged to the person

source_quote: If you are registered unemployed, providing you receive unemployment benefits you are automatically insured via the Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund (Suva) in case of accident. The premium is deducted from your benefits.
notes: Traps Suva for health insurance (B) and the employer-pays pattern that the same page gives for employees (C).

question: Under Swiss compulsory accident insurance, what does an insured person pay towards accident-related medical expenses?

options.A: The annual deductible only, with no retention fee
options.B: A retention fee only, with no deductible
options.C: Nothing - no deductible and no retention fee
options.D: Both the annual deductible and the retention fee, as under basic health insurance

source_quote: Your accident insurance will reimburse accident-related medical expenses. You do not have to pay a deductible or retention fee yourself.
notes: Traps transplanting the KVG franchise/retention structure into accident cover; the page's following sentence makes clear that paying the deductible and retention fee applies only when insured against accident via the health insurer.

question: An accident insurer pays a daily allowance of less than 80 per cent of an employee's salary. What must the employer do under Swiss accident insurance rules?

options.A: Pay nothing further, because the insurer's allowance replaces the salary
options.B: Make up the difference and continue paying full salary in any case
options.C: Make up the difference, but for a maximum of three days only
options.D: Make up the difference, and if the allowance already reaches 80 per cent or more, stop paying salary

source_quote: If the allowance paid by your accident insurance is lower than this figure, your employer must make up the difference. If your insurance benefits correspond to 80% of your salary or more, your employer does not have to continue paying your salary.
notes: The quote's 'this figure' resolves to 80 per cent in the preceding sentence. Traps the assumption that the employer tops up on top of a continuing salary, and the three-day figure from the daily allowance's waiting period.

question: In Switzerland, is a resident free to take compulsory basic health insurance with any authorised insurer operating in the region where they live?

options.A: Yes - any authorised insurer operating in the region, because insurers must offer basic insurance to everyone
options.B: No - the canton assigns each municipality a single designated insurer
options.C: No - only insurers operating in the person's canton of residence may be chosen
options.D: Yes, but only while the insurer still has spare capacity to accept new basic-policy holders

source_quote: You can choose any company that operates in the region where you live. Simply register, because they are required to offer everyone basic insurance.
notes: Traps the canton-assigns-the-insurer model common in neighbouring systems, and the underwriting-capacity model used for supplementary cover on the same page.

question: Which authority decides whether a foreign retiree, student or diplomat living in Switzerland has to take out compulsory health insurance?

options.A: The Federal Social Insurance Office alone, without any canton involved
options.B: The relevant agency in the person's canton or municipality, which approves any exemptions
options.C: The person's employer or scholarship body
options.D: The municipality in which the person was born

source_quote: Foreign retirees, students and diplomats do not necessarily need to take out health insurance. The relevant agency in your canton or municipality approves any exemptions.
notes: Tests where the decision sits in Swiss federalism: canton/municipality, not the federal office and not an employer. Traps a purely federal or purely contractual decision.

question: In Switzerland, may compulsory basic insurance and voluntary supplementary insurance be held with different health insurers?

options.A: No - both must be held with the same insurer
options.B: Yes, but only if both insurers operate in the same canton
options.C: Yes
options.D: Yes, but supplementary cover may not be kept once basic cover is switched

source_quote: You can take out compulsory basic insurance and voluntary supplementary insurance from different health insurers.
notes: Traps the bundled-policy intuition common in other systems; the page adds that switching basic cover lets you keep supplementary cover where it is.

question: What must an applicant normally complete before a Swiss insurer will approve voluntary supplementary health insurance?

options.A: A medical examination at the insurer's expense
options.B: A declaration of their assets and income
options.C: Approval from a cantonal health authority
options.D: A questionnaire on their health

source_quote: As a rule you will have to complete a questionnaire on your health before an insurer will approve supplementary health insurance for you.
notes: Traps the open-enrolment rule for BASIC insurance: insurers must accept everyone for basic cover but may underwrite supplementary cover.

question: Must a Swiss compulsory health insurer offer the whole range of optional deductible levels?

options.A: No - it does not have to offer the full range
options.B: Yes - offering every optional deductible level is a legal requirement
options.C: Yes for adults, but not for children
options.D: Yes, but only in cantons where at least two insurers operate

question: For which age group may a Swiss compulsory health insurer offer deductibles that differ from those it offers to adults?

options.A: Children below the age of 18
options.B: Young adults between the ages of 19 and 25
options.C: Adults over the age of 65
options.D: Persons in education or training of any age

source_quote: It may offer different deductibles for adults and young adults (between the ages of 19 and 25).
notes: Tests the 19-25 young-adult band specifically; children are a separate deductible range on the same page and education/training is the hospital-contribution exemption on S020, so both are confident wrong picks.
